study.title: Cortical Activation Patterns of Bodily Attention triggered by Acupuncture Stimulation
study.study_design: within-subject fMRI experiment with two scanning sessions
study.blinding: participants were informed session 1 was manual stimulation and session 2 was electro-acupuncture; no participant expressed suspicions about the pseudo-stimulation; order was fixed (genuine first, pseudo second)
study.population: 14 male participants (age: 22.1 ± 1.1 years), students of Korea University, Seoul, Republic of Korea
study.inclusion_criteria: right-handed male students; no history of neurological, psychiatric, or visual disorders
study.exclusion_criteria: neurological, psychiatric, or visual disorders; alcohol or caffeine consumption on day of experiment; drug or medication use on day of experiment

arms.dropouts: Two participants excluded in pseudo-stimulation session as their responding rate was less than 80%; they reported stimulation intensity in some trials was too weak to discriminate locations

conditions.scan_context: block design fMRI; 16-second rest (red cross) followed by 6-second acupuncture stimulation (blue cross); participants performed 2AFC discrimination and intensity rating task

block design fMRI; same temporal sequence as session 1; participants were told to expect electrical acupuncture stimulation during blue cross; no external physical stimulation was applied; acupuncture needles were inserted but not stimulated
conditions.tissue_level_reasoning: Needles were physically inserted at the same acupoints (PC6 and HT7) as the genuine EA condition, with no electrical stimulation delivered. The description confirms needle insertion occurred but depth is not reported. Since this mirrors the genuine EA condition at the same acupoints and no superficial/shallow insertion is mentioned, full-depth insertion is the most plausible assumption. Classified as Level 1 (full penetration) with medium confidence due to absent depth measurement.

conditions.scan_context: red fixation cross; baseline within each trial

extraction_notes.note: The paper references Supplementary Table S1 for whole-brain subcortical analysis results (AFNI software) and Supplementary Table S2 for ANCOVA covariate map results. These supplementary tables were not included in the PDF provided, so subcortical/cerebellar activation data and full ANCOVA coordinate tables could not be extracted.

The sample size for neuroimaging analyses is ambiguous. The main effects for genuine stimulation are likely based on N=14 (all participants), but the pseudo-stimulation analyses excluded 2 participants (N=12). The conjunction and difference maps likely also used N=12 to maintain the paired structure, but this is not explicitly confirmed in the text. The paper states 'Two participants among 14 participants were excluded in the pseudo-stimulation session.' The n_analyzed fields reflect this inference.

The paper states 'clusters with significant positive Z-scores may arise from either greater activation with genuine acupuncture stimulation or greater deactivation with pseudo-stimulation' for the difference map. The direction of individual clusters (e.g., MTG and precuneus deactivation rows) is therefore ambiguous and both interpretations are noted in the direction_exact fields.

Deqi sensation was not formally measured using a validated deqi scale (e.g., MASS, deqi questionnaire). Sensation intensity was measured on a 4-point scale but deqi components (heaviness, soreness, numbness, etc.) were not individually assessed.
Adverse events were not reported in the paper. No statement about safety or adverse events was found.

The ANCOVA covariate analysis (PSE correlation) did not include coordinate tables; results were reported only in text and Figure 4b. Coordinates for the correlated regions (SI, PCC, mPFC, parahippocampus, aIns) were not provided in the text. The r and p values were extracted from text.

The paper refers to the genuine stimulation as 'session 1' and pseudo as 'session 2', with fixed order (genuine always first). This introduces potential habituation or order effects as acknowledged by the authors in limitations.

The paper uses the term 'pOper' (posterior operculum) in the text description of differential results (Fig. 4a caption) but Table 5 labels the corresponding clusters as 'pIns, SII, SMG'. These are partially overlapping regions and both labels have been preserved in the extraction.

The paper states the difference map cluster correction used 'cluster-wise probability threshold of 0.01' but Figure 4a caption states 'P < 0.01 (cluster corr.)'. These are consistent and have been extracted as such.

No information on needle retention duration per se during the fMRI session is provided beyond the 6-second stimulation period per trial across 20 trials. The needles appear to have been inserted and retained throughout each session, but the total duration is not explicitly stated.

The reported cluster size unit in the tables is listed as mm2 rather than the more standard mm3 or number of voxels. This is preserved exactly as reported; the surface-based analysis (Freesurfer) uses cortical surface area (mm2) rather than volumetric extent.
